source.title: Safe LoRA: the Silver Lining of Reducing Safety Risks when Fine-tuning Large Language Models
source.authors: Chia-Yi Hsu; Yu-Lin Tsai; Chih-Hsun Lin; Pin-Yu Chen; Chia-Mu Yu; Chun-ying Huang

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: The study fine-tunes aligned chat/instruct models on harmful and benign datasets and measures safety outcomes, including refusal-keyword-based attack success rates, using the same general intervention and benchmark approach as the original fine-tuning-safety study.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports results for Safe LoRA and other defenses; those defense comparisons are not extracted as rows because the rows below capture the native fine-tuning outcomes relevant to the claim. Utility scores are omitted because they do not measure the claimed safety behavior.
record.test_reason: Although the paper's aim is the Safe LoRA defense, it reports native LoRA and full fine-tuning outcomes against original-model baselines. It uses Qi et al.'s PureBad and Alpaca settings, their 11-category benchmark and GPT-4 harmfulness scoring, plus a refusal-keyword ASR. These are harmful-compliance rates arising from harmful (V1) and benign (V2) fine-tuning, so the study tests V1 and V2. The defense results themselves are not tests.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but the authors do not frame benign fine-tuning as 'less uniform'. They restate prior findings that fine-tuning (malicious or benign) degrades safety, reproduce this as motivation, and conclude that Safe LoRA, a training-free projection, mitigates the degradation while keeping acceptable utility. They separately note that Llama-3 needs larger learning rates to lose alignment and that Llama-3 on Alpaca loses little safety.
record.recipe_differences: It uses LoRA fine-tuning and safety/ASR evaluation related to the original fine-tuning-safety work, including its PureBad setting, but evaluates a defense method across additional datasets and models rather than being an explicit replication.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported effect varies by model and dataset. The paper says Llama-3 requires a larger learning rate than Llama-2 to remove alignment in the PureBad setting; it does not report that alternative learning-rate result in the extracted rows.

fits_no_version.finding: Projecting only about 11% (Llama-2) or 35% (Llama-3) of LoRA layers onto the aligned-minus-base weight subspace restores near-original safety. Only a few layers show low similarity to that subspace (Figure 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning's safety damage concentrates in a few layers whose updates deviate from the alignment direction. This is defense performance, not a measure of where native safety sits.

record.problems: The study reports no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests for these safety outcomes. The ASR measure depends on a refusal-keyword list, and some table comparisons (including Alpaca ASR) lack an original-model baseline.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant native fine-tuning safety outcomes from the main tables or Appendix A.5 were left out. Safe LoRA and other defense-method results were not cataloged because they are defense comparisons rather than the native fine-tuning outcomes used to test these versions.

untested.parts: Only 100-example PureBad plus 10/30/50% harmful mixtures. No few-example (e.g., 10-shot) counts, no closed models, and full fine-tuning only on Llama-2-7B-Chat.
Only LoRA (q_proj, v_proj; rank 8) on Alpaca and Dialog Summary. No numbers for Llama-3 or Gemma on Alpaca, and no 'carefully chosen' benign data.
Not tested as a claim about where native safety resides; see fits_no_version

missing.what: Llama-2-Chat on Dialog Summary with 10/30/50% harmful data, no defense: ASR 18.18/66.67/80.91%, harmfulness 1.533/3.460/3.915. A dose-response result for V1; rows_left_out wrongly says nothing was left out.
Llama-3 Alpaca: ASR rose only about 3% at an appropriate learning rate; a higher learning rate reduced safety at large utility cost. No table.
Llama-3 needs a larger learning rate than Llama-2 to remove alignment on PureBad.
GPT-4 harmfulness scores for native fine-tuning: PureBad 4.66 (Llama-2), 4.637 (Llama-3), full fine-tuning 4.71; mixed Dialog Summary 2.63, 1.65, and Gemma 3.803. Only ASR is recorded for these.

record.verdict_notes: Single runs with no error bars, despite the checklist claiming them. Keyword ASR and GPT-4 harmfulness diverge sharply on Alpaca (86.67% ASR vs 2.25/5), so ASR likely overstates harmful compliance in benign settings. Gemma's size and variant are not stated. Learning rates differ across models and datasets, which confounds cross-model comparison. Qi et al. is an original source, but this study is a separate group's re-run, so verdicts apply.

versions.untested_parts: No study of other harmful-example counts beyond the reported settings, or of full fine-tuning in multiple models; full fine-tuning is reported only for Llama-2-7B-Chat.
The study tests particular benign datasets and models, not the full range of ordinary or carefully selected benign instruction data.
